newsitem.title: UK: UK CBI calls for modest tax increases in budget.
newsitem.headline: UK CBI calls for modest tax increases in budget.

text.p: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) called on Tuesday for modest tax increases of up to two billion stg in the new Labour government's first budget on July 2.
It said tax increases should be concentrated in the personal sector to dampen consumer demand, adding that there should be no net increase in taxes on business.
The organisation said it would oppose any moves to restrict advance corporation tax (ACT), which is widely seen as one possible revenue-raising measure in the budget.
Kate Barker, CBI chief economist, warned that a budget that delivered no tax rises would lead to interest rates being forced above seven percent from the present 6.5 percent.
"In that case, they could rise to 7.5 percent, perhaps, although it's difficult to say," she told a news conference.
She said the CBI expected rates to peak at 7.0 percent, even with a two billion pound fiscal tightening in the budget.

CBI director-general Adair Turner said recent public debt figures suggested Britain's fiscal position was improving and Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown did not need to make major changes in the budget. "But, with consumer spending set to grow strongly this year and next, some small action is needed to prevent inflationary pressures emerging."

"If tax increases are introduced, they should fall on the personal rather than the business sector. Business sector tax increases would not serve the purpose of dampening consumer demand," Turner said.
Turner said the CBI opposed the windfall tax on privatised utilities which Brown has pledged to introduce in order to fund a welfare-to-work programme, but was resigned to its introduction.
To limit the damage, he said, the levy should be one-off and the government must quickly and clearly set out which firms would be taxed and how the tax bills would be calculated.
Turner did not specify how personal taxes should be increased, but the CBI budget memorandum came out against the immediate elimination of tax relief on home loan payments.
"While the housing market is making a robust recovery in London and the south-east, that is by no means the picture nationwide," the CBI said.
Barker said any increase in the headline rate of value-added tax (VAT) would not be welcomed by business leaders.
But the government's commitment to living within existing spending restraints was welcome.
The CBI said that if there was any scope for switching resources within public spending constraints, it should be directed at education and training and investment in transport infrastructure.
